passage:
Warden's note, hostel B, Wednesday night. Jagdish knocked on my door at ten, phone in hand. He had sent a message to his friend Imtiaz at lunch about the group assignment and there had been no reply for eight hours. "I keep thinking he is angry about the presentation," he said. I asked what he could do with the worry other than carry it around. He thought for a minute, then typed, "Hey, are you annoyed with me, or am I imagining it? No pressure to reply fast." He showed me before sending. Imtiaz answered in minutes: his phone had been charging in the lab. Jagdish laughed, read the reply twice and went back to his room.
Mahima, hostel warden

qa.q: How long had Jagdish waited for a reply from Imtiaz?
qa.a: Jagdish had waited about eight hours with no reply.

qa.q: What was Jagdish afraid of when knocking on the warden's door?
qa.a: Jagdish was afraid that Imtiaz was angry about the presentation. The worry had built up over eight hours of silence.

qa.q: What did Jagdish do instead of building a story from the silence?
qa.a: Jagdish asked Imtiaz directly whether he was annoyed or imagining it, and added that there was no pressure to reply fast. The gentle, direct question ended the worry.

qa.q: What might Imtiaz have seen when the question arrived?
qa.a: Imtiaz may have seen a kind, honest message from a friend who cared, with room to answer. Imtiaz had only left the phone charging in the lab.

grounding: A young adult asks a friend directly and gently whether the friend is upset, rather than building a story from a delayed reply.

passage:
9:40 pm. My friend Sangeeta has not answered my message since morning. I only asked whether she would join the study group on Friday. By noon I had decided she was tired of me. By four I had a whole story: I talked too much last week, I forgot to thank her for the notes, she is pulling away. My chest hurt at dinner, and I barely tasted the food.
Then I thought, that is a lot of story for zero facts. So I wrote, "Hey, I have not heard from you and my brain is spinning. Are you cross with me, or is this just my imagination? 🙂"
She replied in five minutes: cousin's wedding, no signal all day. Sorry! Friday yes.
I feel silly and light. Note to self: ask sooner.
— Nilesh

qa.q: When did Nilesh write this diary entry?
qa.a: Nilesh wrote at 9:40 pm.

qa.q: How was Nilesh feeling by four o'clock and what shows it?
qa.a: Nilesh felt anxious and hurt, sure that Sangeeta was pulling away. The whole story about talking too much and forgetting to thank her for the notes shows the worry spiralling.

qa.q: What did Nilesh do that stopped the spiral?
qa.a: Nilesh noticed the story had zero facts and asked Sangeeta directly whether she was upset or if it was imagination. The question got an answer within five minutes.

qa.q: What was Sangeeta's day like before the reply?
qa.a: Sangeeta was at a cousin's wedding with no signal all day, so had no chance to answer. It had nothing to do with the study group or with Nilesh.

grounding: A young adult asks directly and gently whether a friend is upset instead of building a story from a delayed reply.

passage:
Dolma: hey, did you get my message about Saturday?
[4 hours later]
Dolma: Elizabeth, can I ask something without it being weird
Elizabeth: sure
Dolma: have I upset you, or am I making it up in my head? you usually reply fast and since the café thing I've felt a gap
Elizabeth: oh no
Elizabeth: not upset at all. my grandmother's been in and out of hospital this week, I've barely looked at my phone
Dolma: I'm so sorry. I'm glad I asked instead of stewing
Elizabeth: me too honestly. I did think you'd be annoyed that I went quiet
Dolma: never. do you want to skip Saturday?
Elizabeth: can we do Sunday instead, just a walk?
Dolma: Sunday walk it is 🤍
Elizabeth: thank you for checking 🙏

qa.q: What had been happening in Elizabeth's week?
qa.a: Elizabeth's grandmother had been in and out of hospital, and Elizabeth had barely looked at the phone.

qa.q: What was Dolma feeling before asking the question?
qa.a: Dolma felt uneasy and a little hurt, sensing a gap since the café and worrying that Elizabeth was upset with Dolma.

qa.q: Why was Dolma's question a good one?
qa.a: It was direct and gentle, allowing either answer, so it ended the guessing and let Elizabeth share what was really going on.

qa.q: How did Elizabeth feel when Dolma asked?
qa.a: Elizabeth felt relieved and grateful 🙏, having worried that Dolma would be annoyed at the silence.

grounding: A young adult asks gently whether a friend is upset or it is imagined, instead of spiralling over a delayed reply.

passage:
In their small town, the evening bus from the college only came once an hour, and Joseph was waiting at the stand under the neem tree. Since morning he had heard nothing from Vikas, who always replied in minutes. They'd argued about the cricket team captaincy the day before.
Joseph's thoughts started stacking: Vikas is sulking. Vikas has made new friends. Vikas thinks I'm arrogant.
He caught himself. That was a whole story built from one silent phone.
He typed: "Did I upset you yesterday, or am I just imagining things?"
He added: "Either way is fine to say."
The bus came, and at the third stop his phone buzzed.
"Not upset, da. Papa needed help in the sugarcane field, and the phone was in the tractor. Captaincy thing, we'll sort tomorrow."
Joseph laughed out loud, and an old man across the aisle smiled at him.

qa.q: Where was Joseph waiting?
qa.a: Joseph was waiting at the bus stand under the neem tree.

qa.q: What was Joseph worried about before he typed his question?
qa.a: Joseph was anxious that Vikas was sulking about the captaincy argument or thought he was arrogant, building fears from a silent phone.

qa.q: What would you advise someone in Joseph's place?
qa.a: Do what Joseph did: notice the story you are building, then ask a short, gentle question that makes either answer easy to give.

qa.q: How did Vikas likely see the whole situation?
qa.a: Vikas was simply busy in the sugarcane field and not upset, so Vikas may have been surprised Joseph worried at all.

grounding: A young adult asks gently whether a friend is upset instead of building a story from a delayed reply, and the spiral stops.

passage:
Tariq had sent Tuan the draft of their housing proposal at nine in the morning. By four, on the tram home through rainy Melbourne, there was still nothing. Tuan usually answered within the hour, often with a joke.
Tariq's mind began doing its thing. He hates the draft. He's rewriting it without me. He's still annoyed that I spoke over him at the tutorial.
Tariq caught his reflection in the tram window, frowning, and nearly laughed. He'd written half a drama in his head from an empty inbox.
He texted: "Hey, quick question, no pressure. Did I annoy you, or am I just imagining it?"
Ten minutes later: "Imagining it, mate 😄 I had two lab shifts back to back. Reading your draft now. Also, sorry about the tutorial, I interrupted you first."
Tariq put the phone away, his chest loosening as the tram swung around the corner.

qa.q: How long had Tariq waited without a reply?
qa.a: He sent the draft at nine in the morning, and by four there was still nothing.

qa.q: What does Tariq's frown in the tram window suggest about how he was feeling?
qa.a: It suggests he was tense and anxious, spinning fears that Tuan hated the draft or was still annoyed about the tutorial.

qa.q: What went well in how Tariq handled it?
qa.a: He noticed his own spiral, then asked a direct, low-pressure question instead of acting on his guesses.

qa.q: How did Tuan see the delay?
qa.a: Tuan saw it as just a busy day with two lab shifts, and even felt a bit sorry about interrupting Tariq at the tutorial.

grounding: A young adult outside India asks directly whether a friend is upset rather than spiralling over a delayed reply.

passage: In the hostel mess, Lavanya kept flipping her phone over between bites of upma. She had messaged Mehak at eight: "Still on for the library at 4?" It was now past one, and Mehak had been online twice. Lavanya's mind began building a case: the charger she hadn't returned, the joke about Mehak's presentation on Monday that maybe landed wrong. By the time she reached her tea she had half-drafted apologies for three different things. Then she put down her spoon and typed instead: "Hey, quick check, have I upset you, or am I just overthinking? 🙂" She sent it before she could soften it into nothing. Twelve minutes later: "Omg no!! Lab ran over and my phone was on 2%. Library at 4 still yes. And your joke was funny btw." Lavanya let out a long breath and actually tasted her upma.

qa.q: At what time had Lavanya messaged Mehak?
qa.a: She had messaged Mehak at eight.

qa.q: What does Lavanya flipping her phone over suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she was anxious and restless, already worried that the delay meant Mehak was upset with her.

qa.q: Which choice helped Lavanya most, and why?
qa.a: Sending one gentle, direct question instead of drafting apologies stopped the spiral and brought the real reason within twelve minutes.

qa.q: Why might Mehak have been glad to get the direct question?
qa.a: Mehak could clear things up in one reply, before a delay caused by a long lab and a dying phone turned into hurt feelings.

grounding: Shows a young adult who stops building a story from a delayed reply and asks one direct, gentle question instead.
